The Case for Restricting Scientology: When Religious Freedom Becomes a Shield for Abuse

Introduction

Religious liberty stands as one of the most cherished principles in democratic societies. Enshrined in the First Amendment of the United States Constitution and protected by international human rights declarations, the freedom to believe, worship, and organize according to one's conscience represents a hard-won triumph of Enlightenment values. However, this liberty was never intended to be absolute, nor was it designed to provide an impenetrable legal fortress behind which organizations could systematically abuse, exploit, defraud, and imprison human beings with impunity. The Church of Scientology, founded by science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard in the 1950s, represents precisely the kind of organization that tests the limits of religious freedom—and exposes its vulnerabilities. When examined through the lens of documented evidence, survivor testimony, judicial findings, and investigative journalism spanning decades, the conclusion becomes difficult to avoid: Scientology operates not as a legitimate religion deserving of legal protection, but as a dangerous, coercive organization that uses the veneer of religious practice to engage in systematic human rights abuses, financial exploitation, and psychological manipulation. Governments should accordingly reclassify, heavily regulate, or in some cases ban its organizational operations—not to persecute belief, but to protect citizens from demonstrable harm.

I. The Historical Foundation: A "Religion" Engineered for Profit and Power

Any serious analysis of Scientology must begin with its origins, which reveal an organization designed from inception not around sincere spiritual inquiry, but around profit, control, and the personal aggrandizement of its founder.

L. Ron Hubbard was a prolific science fiction writer of middling commercial success before he published Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health in 1950. The book presented a pseudoscientific system of mental therapy that Hubbard claimed could cure everything from poor eyesight to mental illness. When the American Psychological Association and the medical establishment rejected Dianetics as unfounded, and when Hubbard's Dianetics organizations began failing financially, Hubbard made a pivotal strategic decision: he repackaged his system as a religion.

The cynicism of this move was not hidden. Multiple contemporaries of Hubbard reported him stating, in various formulations, that the real way to make money was to start a religion. Writer Lloyd Eshbach recounted in his autobiography Over My Shoulder that Hubbard told him, "I'd like to start a religion. That's where the money is." Harlan Ellison, Sam Moskowitz, and other science fiction contemporaries reported similar statements. While Scientology disputes these accounts, the documentary record tells its own story: Hubbard created a religious framework precisely when it became financially and legally advantageous to do so, gaining tax exemptions and protections that a for-profit therapeutic business could never claim.

This origin matters because it speaks to institutional DNA. Scientology was not born from genuine revelation, spiritual tradition, or communal practice. It was engineered as a control mechanism—and that engineering has defined the organization ever since.

II. Financial Exploitation: A System of Extraction

One of the most well-documented aspects of Scientology is its extraordinary system of financial extraction from members, which goes far beyond the tithing or voluntary donations characteristic of mainstream religions.

Scientology operates on a pay-per-service model in which members must purchase increasingly expensive courses and "auditing" sessions to advance through the organization's spiritual hierarchy. The so-called "Bridge to Total Freedom"—the prescribed path of spiritual advancement—costs members hundreds of thousands of dollars to complete. Estimates from former members and investigative journalists place the total cost at anywhere from $300,000 to over $500,000, with some members reporting expenditures exceeding $1 million over their lifetimes.

This is not voluntary generosity. The system is structured to make advancement contingent on payment. Members who cannot pay are pressured to take out loans, drain savings accounts, refinance homes, and even borrow from family members. The organization employs dedicated "registrars" whose sole function is to extract maximum financial commitments from members, using high-pressure sales techniques that would be illegal if employed by secular businesses in many jurisdictions.

Former senior executive Jeff Hawkins has described being personally pressured to spend his entire life savings. Journalist Janet Reitman, in her extensively researched book Inside Scientology, documented case after case of members driven into financial ruin. The organization also requires members to purchase Hubbard's books and lectures repeatedly—even when they already own them—every time new "edited" editions are released.

When members attempt to leave, they are presented with "freeloader bills"—invoices for the full retail price of every course or service they received while working for the organization, sometimes totaling tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. This practice functions as financial coercion designed to trap people within the system.

No legitimate religion systematically bankrupts its adherents as a condition of spiritual participation. This is the business model of a predatory commercial enterprise hiding behind a cross.

III. The Abuse of Human Beings: The Rehabilitation Project Force and Sea Organization

Perhaps the most disturbing aspect of Scientology's operations is the treatment of members within its Sea Organization (Sea Org), the organization's dedicated clergy, and particularly within the Rehabilitation Project Force (RPF), its internal punishment program.

The Sea Organization

Sea Org members sign billion-year contracts—a symbolic but psychologically binding commitment—and work for the organization under conditions that multiple governments, journalists, and former members have described as forced labor. Sea Org members routinely work 80 to 100+ hours per week. They receive minimal compensation—often reported as $50 per week or less, sometimes as little as $15. They live in communal, often substandard housing controlled by the organization. Their mail is monitored, their phone calls restricted, and their contact with the outside world severely limited.

Members who wish to leave face an elaborate "routing out" process designed to delay and discourage departure, including extensive interrogation sessions (called "sec checks") using Scientology's E-meter device. Those who leave without authorization are declared "Suppressive Persons"—Scientology's version of excommunication—which triggers the policy of disconnection, severing all ties with family and friends who remain in the organization.

The International Labour Organization's conventions on forced labor identify key indicators: restriction of movement, debt bondage, withholding of wages, and psychological coercion. The Sea Organization meets virtually every one of these criteria.

The Rehabilitation Project Force

The RPF is Scientology's internal prison system, and that characterization is not hyperbolic. Members assigned to the RPF—often for questioning leadership, underperforming, or expressing doubt—are subjected to conditions that constitute imprisonment and abuse by any reasonable standard:

  • Physical confinement: RPF members are confined to specific areas and cannot leave without permission. At the organization's international headquarters in Hemet, California (known as "Gold Base"), former members have described razor wire, motion sensors, and security personnel preventing departure.

  • Forced labor: RPF members perform heavy manual labor—construction, cleaning, renovation—for 30 or more hours per week, in addition to mandatory Scientology study and confessional sessions.

  • Sleep deprivation: Former RPF members report being permitted as few as four to six hours of sleep per night.

  • Restricted communication: RPF members cannot speak to non-RPF members unless spoken to first. They cannot contact family. They are, for all practical purposes, disappeared from the lives of people who care about them.

  • Duration: Assignment to the RPF is indefinite. Some members have spent years—even over a decade—in the program. Marc Headley, in his memoir Blown for Good, described conditions at Gold Base that included physical violence, sleep deprivation, and confinement.

These are not allegations from hostile outsiders. They come from dozens of former senior members, including Mike Rinder (former head of the Office of Special Affairs), Marty Rathbun (former Inspector General of the Religious Technology Center), Amy Scobee, Tom DeVocht, and many others who held positions of authority within the organization before leaving. Their accounts are remarkably consistent across decades and continents.

IV. The Policy of Disconnection: Systematic Destruction of Families

Scientology's disconnection policy is one of its most cruel and well-documented practices. Under this policy, members who are connected to individuals declared "Suppressive Persons" (SPs) are required to sever all contact with those individuals—or face being declared SPs themselves.

In practice, this means that when a member leaves Scientology or speaks critically about the organization, their family members who remain in Scientology are forced to cut them off completely. Parents lose contact with children. Siblings stop speaking. Marriages are destroyed.

The human toll is staggering. Leah Remini, in her Emmy-winning documentary series Scientology and the Aftermath, presented case after case of families torn apart by this policy. Ron Miscavige, father of current Scientology leader David Miscavige, has described being cut off from his son and other family members. Hundreds of former members have publicly shared similar stories.

Scientology officially claims that disconnection is a personal choice made voluntarily by members. This is disingenuous to the point of dishonesty. When the consequence of maintaining a family relationship is the loss of every other relationship, one's community, one's spiritual framework, and potentially one's livelihood (since many Scientologists work for Scientology-owned businesses or fellow Scientologists), the "choice" is no choice at all. It is coercion operating through the threat of total social annihilation.

Mainstream religions may disapprove of apostasy, but the systematic, institutionally enforced severing of family bonds as an instrument of organizational control places Scientology in the company of the most destructive cults in modern history.

V. Fair Game: The Weaponization of Litigation and Harassment

Scientology has a long and extensively documented history of using litigation, private investigation, intimidation, and outright harassment to silence critics, punish defectors, and destroy perceived enemies. This pattern of behavior is not incidental—it is doctrinal, rooted in Hubbard's own policies.

Hubbard's Written Policies

Hubbard's policy letter on "Suppressive Persons" stated that SPs "may be deprived of property or injured by any means by any Scientologist without any discipline of the Scientologist. May be tricked, sued, or lied to or destroyed." Though Scientology claims this policy (known as "Fair Game") was officially cancelled in 1968, multiple courts and former officials have found that only the label was cancelled—the practices continued unabated.

Operation Snow White

In the 1970s, Scientology conducted the single largest infiltration of the United States government in history. Under the direction of Hubbard's wife Mary Sue Hubbard and the organization's Guardian's Office, Scientology operatives infiltrated 136 government agencies, including the IRS, FBI, CIA, and Department of Justice. They stole tens of thousands of documents, bugged government offices, and attempted to destroy records unfavorable to Scientology. Eleven senior Scientology officials, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted of conspiracy, theft of government documents, and obstruction of justice.

This was not the action of a few rogue members. It was a coordinated, organization-wide criminal conspiracy directed from the highest levels of leadership.

Ongoing Harassment

The pattern has continued for decades. Journalist Paulette Cooper, who wrote The Scandal of Scientology in 1971, was subjected to a Scientology operation (Operation Freakout) designed to have her "incarcerated in a mental institution or jail" by framing her for bomb threats. The plan was documented in Scientology's own seized files.

More recently, former members who have spoken publicly—including Leah Remini, Mike Rinder, and numerous others—have reported being followed by private investigators, having their homes surveilled, being subjected to frivolous lawsuits, and enduring organized harassment campaigns. In 2024, Scientology filed a barrage of lawsuits against former members and critics that many legal observers characterized as strategic litigation designed to silence opposition (SLAPP suits).

Any organization that systematically deploys criminal activity and harassment against critics is not exercising religious freedom—it is engaging in organized intimidation that merits legal intervention.

VI. The Tax-Exempt Status: A Case Study in Institutional Intimidation

Scientology's acquisition of tax-exempt status in the United States in 1993—after decades of being denied it—stands as one of the most troubling episodes in American regulatory history and illustrates the organization's willingness to bully government institutions into submission.

After losing its tax-exempt status in 1967, Scientology waged a decades-long war against the IRS. The organization filed over 2,000 lawsuits against the agency. Individual Scientology members filed thousands more against individual IRS employees. Private investigators were hired to dig up personal information on IRS officials. The campaign of litigation and intimidation was so intense and so costly that in 1993, the IRS capitulated and granted tax-exempt status in a secret closing agreement—the terms of which were not made public until forced by The New York Times through litigation.

This was not a legitimate determination of religious bona fides. It was an agency surrendering to an adversary that had made the cost of continued resistance unbearable. The exemption has since shielded billions of dollars in Scientology assets and income from taxation, depriving the public of revenue while funding the very operations described above.

Other countries have reached different conclusions. Germany's domestic intelligence agency has monitored Scientology for decades, classifying it as a threat to democratic order rather than a religion. France convicted Scientology of organized fraud in 2009. Belgium charged Scientology with fraud and extortion. Russia banned Scientology's Moscow branch. These countries are not theocratic backwaters hostile to religious freedom—they are modern democracies that examined Scientology's operations and concluded that they warranted legal restriction rather than religious protection.

VII. Addressing the Religious Freedom Objection

The most significant argument against restricting Scientology is the religious freedom objection: that any government action against a self-described religious organization sets a dangerous precedent that could be used against legitimate faiths. This concern is not trivial, and it deserves a serious response.

First, the argument presented here is not that Scientology should be restricted because its beliefs are strange, unscientific, or objectionable. A society committed to religious freedom must tolerate beliefs that seem absurd or offensive to the majority. If Scientologists wish to believe in thetans, Xenu, or the spiritual efficacy of auditing, they are entitled to do so, and the state has no business evaluating the truth or falsity of those beliefs.

The argument is that Scientology should be restricted because of what it does, not what it believes. The practices described in this essay—financial exploitation, forced labor, imprisonment, family destruction, criminal activity, systematic harassment—are not expressions of religious belief. They are violations of civil and criminal law, and no organization should be permitted to commit them simply by claiming religious motivation.

We already accept this principle in other contexts. A religion that practiced human sacrifice would not be permitted to do so, regardless of the sincerity of belief. Parents who deny medical care to children on religious grounds have been prosecuted for negligence and manslaughter. Religious organizations whose leaders sexually abuse members are subject to criminal prosecution. The principle is clear and well-established: religious freedom protects belief and worship, not the infliction of harm.

Second, restricting Scientology's organizational operations would not require evaluating theological claims. It would require applying existing laws—against fraud, forced labor, false imprisonment, harassment, and coercion—to an organization that has systematically violated them. The failure to do so is not religious tolerance; it is selective non-enforcement of the law, and it sends the message that wrapping abuse in religious language renders it immune from legal consequences.

Third, the slippery slope argument—that restricting Scientology will lead to restricting Catholicism, Islam, or Buddhism—fails because it ignores the specificity of the evidence. The case against Scientology is not based on theological disagreement but on decades of documented, corroborated, adjudicated criminal and abusive conduct.
